newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices bottom out after two-week slide.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices bottom out after two-week slide.

text.p: World oil markets steadied on Friday, bringing to an end a two-week slide which has knocked nearly 10 percent off the price of a barrel of Brent, traders said.
Strikes by oilworkers in Colombia and Venezuela helped underpin the bellwether crude, trimming recent losses prompted by evidence of waning demand for winter heating fuel and surging supply.
April Brent on the International Petroleum Exchange in London closed 16 cents higher at $20.49 a barrel.
"There were plenty of good reasons for the market selling off and plenty of good reasons for it to bottom out," said Peter Gignoux, head of the energy desk at brokers Smith Barney.
A four-day strike by public sector workers in Colombia, which led to a 10 percent cut in pumping operations along the country's pipelines on Wednesday, showed no sign of coming to a swift conclusion.
Marathon talks aimed at ending the nationwide strike in support of a 21.5 percent pay claim broke down early on Friday with no sign of an agreement soon, negotiators said.
A pay dispute at Venezuelan state oil company PDVSA escalated into strike action on Friday but the stoppage attracted mixed support and did not affect operations, the company said.
"News of an eight-hour strike in Venezuela with possibly more to come and port closures in Mexico have added support," said Charles Gray of brokers Prudential-Bache.
Dealers said the sharp losses of the past two weeks were also running out of steam as traders looked to lock in profits on their short positions ahead of a three-day weekend in the United States.

"It is true that the move has been a little rapid for comfort and with the President's !Day holiday coming up, there is likely to be some short covering ahead of the weekend," said brokers GNI in a daily report.
But despite the steadier tone on Friday, dealers say the medium-term outlook remains bleak.
The prospect of higher Iraqi oil exports had returned to haunt the market on Wednesday, intensifying downward pressure.

United Nations overseers are considering an allowance for Iraqi sales over and above the original export contracts signed under the U.N.-sponsored oil-for-food agreement to compensate for plummeting oil prices.

A U.N. report put the total value of the first three month's worth of Iraqi sales at about $800 million, against a cash target of $1 billion for the first tranche of exports under the plan to pay for humanitarian aid for the sanctions-bound OPEC nation.

Members of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) pumped 25.38 million barrels per day (bpd) in January, up from 24.98 million in December, the Vienna-based OPEC secretariat said in a monthly report published on Friday.
By comparison, a recent Reuters survey put OPEC output at 26.64 million bpd. The 11-member group has an official ceiling of 25.03 million bpd.
